Category: Object.
Subject: pinball machine.
Style: 1970s space-age.
reasoning:
This is a static object, a 1970s space-age pinball machine, so I'm planning dimensions based on real-world scale—roughly 0.56m wide cabinet, 1.35m long, with legs raising it about 0.7m off the ground—before writing the TypeScript module.

I'm working out a coordinate mapping to translate playfield-local positions (across, along, height) into model space, accounting for the 6.5° tilt where the playfield rises toward the backbox, using basis vectors for the slope direction and surface normal.

I'm setting up a tilt quaternion via rotation about the X axis so that part orientations naturally align with the sloped playfield, plus an extra spin rotation for parts needing independent orientation on the surface. Since this is a static model with no joints needed, I'm confirming that parts placed this way can just sit under the root group without requiring bone attachments.

Now I'm working out physical dimensions in meters for the cabinet and legs so the whole machine stands correctly on the floor — cabinet width around 0.56m, length roughly 1.55m front-to-back, with front legs shorter than back legs to create the tilt, while also considering how the cabinet itself needs to tilt along with the playfield.

I'm working out the tilted playfield geometry numerically — setting the playfield length and tilt angle (6.5°), then computing how much the back raises and front lowers relative to the origin, so I can place the cabinet floor and side rails correctly beneath the sloped surface.

With the cabinet bottom positioned, I'm figuring out leg heights at front and back, then checking if the total height (legs + cabinet + backbox) matches a realistic pinball machine (~1.9-2m). The first pass felt too short, so I'm raising the base height Y0 to 0.9 and recalculating front/back cabinet bottoms and backbox position to get proportions closer to a real cabinet.

I'll keep the design simple: a backbox roughly 0.58 wide, 0.7 tall, 0.2 deep, evoking a 1970s-style unit with an electromechanical score display and a space-themed translite art panel.

Now I'm planning the backglass SVG — rocket, rings, stars, a title like "COSMIC ORBIT," black score windows glowing with digits, plus labels for "PLAYER 1-4," "BALL IN PLAY," "TILT," and "GAME OVER." Then I'll move to the playfield art texture itself.

I'm figuring out how to orient the playfield plane geometry so its face-up normal aligns correctly with the scene, rotating the SVG-textured plane so the artwork reads properly from above.

Let me verify with the cross product: facing -Z with up +Y gives right = +X, confirming the player's right matches +X, consistent with left-to-right SVG mapping. So the model's front at +Z is indeed the player side, and everything checks out.

I'll skip adding glass since there's no transparency control, keeping the playfield open and readable instead -- maybe just the lockdown bar and rails for framing. For layout, I'm setting the inner playfield width to 0.5 units (x from -0.25 to 0.25) and length 1.0 (z from -0.5 at the back to 0.5 at the front), with the cabinet extending outward from there.

Now I'm sizing the cabinet itself: outer width 0.56 with 0.03-thick walls, and length 1.06 to leave room for the front apron panel. For the aesthetic, I'm going with a 1970s-style theme -- deep midnight blue cabinet sides with an orange rocket, stripe, and starburst decal, plus chrome rails and legs, rather than a more space-age silver-orange-turquoise palette.

I'm settling on a cream, atomic orange, turquoise, mustard, navy, and magenta palette with chrome accents for the rails and legs, applying flat colors for painted parts and a polished steel look for the metal pieces. For the pop bumpers, I'm shaping them as mushroom-like lathed forms with a red-orange glowing cap ringed in turquoise.

Now I'm positioning three bumpers in a triangle near a central planet illustration on the upper playfield, with orbit rings decorating the art. Next I'm laying out the two flippers at the lower playfield, defining their pivot points, tapered length, and colored rubber extrusion.

Working out flipper geometry...

Adding the extrude helper logic...

Now I'm positioning the left and right flippers symmetrically, with the left flipper angled downward-inward at about -28° and the right flipper mirrored at 208°, checking how rotating the outline affects its orientation.

For the flippers' look, I'm giving them a cream body with a darker spine inset, a chrome pivot disc, and a red post, plus a thinner orange cap layer on top for that 1970s style. For the slingshots, I'm planning triangular rubber kickers above the flippers with an orange plastic triangle, inlaid star, and thin rod-like rubber bands.

Now I'm working out the exact triangle coordinates for the left slingshot, positioning the vertices so the wall-side edge is vertical and the hypotenuse faces inward toward the flipper.

Working out flipper tip positions so the gap matches a standard ball diameter, giving roughly a 0.05 unit gap. Then I'm roughing in the drain apron and the inlane/outlane guide rod placements, approximating their endpoints near the sling and flipper pivot regions since exact coordinates aren't critical yet.

For the ball, I'll place one in the shooter lane and consider resting another on a flipper, working out its resting height and offset from the pivot.

I'm also planning the shooter lane itself—a thin separator rail near the right wall—plus the plunger mechanism: a rod with a knob extending through the cabinet front, angled correctly within the tilted playfield plane.

Setting up a `pf()` helper to position objects using the playfield's orientation quaternion, with optional local rotations for tilt and spin so pieces like the plunger rod align properly along the playfield surface.

Next I'm planning the standup targets (a row of three on the left) and a drop-target bank of four at upper right, each with colored boxes and chrome brackets, plus a round "special" spot target with a glowing insert. For lit inserts like arrows and stars, I realize applying glow() to the whole playfield texture would make it look backlit rather than having distinct illuminated spots, so I need separate small insert parts instead.

I'm planning round insert discs (thin cylinders) and extruded star/arrow shapes with glow applied individually, maybe a dozen total, plus glowing pop bumper caps and a backlit translite effect on the backbox with glow strength around 0.8-0.9 to simulate lit screens and score windows. Now I'm thinking through the top rollover lanes—three or four lanes with small rollover button discs, rubber guide posts, and a curved arch structure at the top of the playfield.

For the orbit path, I'm sweeping a chrome rail along a curved spline computed from catmull points that trace the ball's route from the shooter lane up through the top curve. Then for the cabinet, I'm laying out tilted side panels as thin boxes with navy paint and SVG decal planes mounted just outside the panel surfaces.

Working through the decal plane orientation, I'm rotating each plane 90 degrees about Y so its face points outward along ±X, checking how the plane's local axes map to the playfield's X/Z directions so the texture reads correctly when viewed from outside the cabinet.

On the +X side the texture's u-axis increases toward the back, meaning left=front and right=back as drawn. On the -X side it's flipped (left=back, right=front), so a rocket texture drawn pointing right would end up facing opposite directions on each side -- I need to mirror the texture on one side so both rockets consistently point toward the back, though there's no built-in mirror option for this.

I'll just generate the mirrored side texture directly with a flipped SVG transform, keeping any text out of that art since mirroring would reverse it. Both rockets will point toward the backbox as if ascending, and next I'm roughing out the bottom front apron panel dimensions.
